html:
The Plague of Justinian was the first recorded pandemic of bubonic plague, which swept the Mediterranean, Europe and the Near East from 541 to 549. It is named after the Roman emperor Justinian I, who caught it in 542 and survived.

The disease first appeared in Egypt in 541 and reached Constantinople, the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire, the next year. The historian Procopius saw it there and described the swellings in the groin and armpit, and so many dead that the city ran out of places to bury them. It also struck the Sasanian Empire in Persia.

DNA from graves in Germany and elsewhere has confirmed that the cause was Yersinia pestis, the same bacterium behind the later Black Death. It spread through fleas on rats along trade and grain routes.

  • The plague came back in waves for about two centuries, among them the plague of Amwas in Syria in 638.
  • How many died is disputed. Older estimates spoke of tens of millions and a collapse of population. Some recent studies argue the damage was smaller and more local.

It struck while Justinian was trying to win back Italy and the western Mediterranean, and some historians think it drained the men and taxes he needed. Some also argue that by weakening both Rome and Persia it helped open the way for the Arab conquests of the 630s. The next great plague pandemic, the Black Death, came eight centuries later.
sum: The Plague of Justinian was the first recorded pandemic of bubonic plague, which swept the Mediterranean, Europe and the Near East from 541 to 549. It is named after the Roman emperor Justinian I, who caught it in 542 and survived.
